Preprocessing raw single-cell data

Jia Ding

2026-11-16

Source: vignettes/preprocess_from_raw_counts.Rmd
preprocess_from_raw_counts.Rmd

1. When you need this vignette

prepare_data() expects a matrix that is already at clone level: one column per clone, or one column per cell plus a cell-to-clone table. If all you have is a raw count matrix straight out of Cell Ranger, use preprocess_sc() first. It turns

genes x cells (raw counts, no QC, no clustering)

into

cell_id, clone_id, patient, cluster_size_class, UMAP coordinates

which is exactly the clone_labels argument of prepare_data().

You do not need to know anything about single-cell analysis to use it. Every threshold is derived from your own data.

2. Inputs

Two things are required:

Argument What it is
counts Genes as rows, cells as columns. Raw counts (integers).
patient_labels One patient ID per cell.

A third is optional but important:

Argument When to supply it
sample_labels A patient has several samples (e.g. biopsies before and after treatment).

If the counts are still in CellRanger files, read_10x() reads a folder, an .h5 file, or the three files directly and returns the matrix described above:

my_counts <- read_10x("path/to/filtered_feature_bc_matrix")
# or: read_10x("path/to/filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5")
# or: read_10x(mtx = "matrix.mtx.gz", barcodes = "barcodes.tsv.gz",
#              features = "features.tsv.gz")
labels <- preprocess_sc(
  counts = my_counts,
  patient_labels = cell_to_patient  # same length as ncol(my_counts)
)

If your matrix is transposed, preprocess_sc() stops with a message telling you to use t(counts) instead of silently producing nonsense.

3. What it does, in order

  1. Quality control. For each patient separately, the gene count gets an upper fence at median + nmads × MAD and the mitochondrial fraction an upper fence at min(median + nmads × MAD, max_mito); the lower gene bound is the absolute min_genes (default 200), not a MAD fence. nmads defaults to
    1. Tumour tissue carries more mitochondrial reads and larger cells than blood, so a narrow 3-MAD fence deletes real cells: on a real lung squamous carcinoma raw matrix, 5 MAD recovers ~88% of the cells CellRanger calls versus ~78% at 3 MAD, with precision unchanged. A hard cap (max_mito, default 25%) prevents the fence from widening on a mostly-bad sample. Pass skip_qc = TRUE when the matrix is already curated (e.g. malignant cells downloaded from a paper): every cell is then kept, which is what the original pipeline does.
  2. Optional doublet removal. Only when remove_doublets = TRUE: cells that scDblFinder calls doublets are dropped, one patient at a time.
  3. Normalisation. LogNormalize with a scale factor of 10,000.
  4. Optional exclusion of non-target cells. Only when exclude_markers is supplied; see section 8.
  5. Variable features and PCA. Computed on all cells together, so distances mean the same thing for every patient.
  6. Clustering. By default all cells are clustered together, as in the original PERCEPTION method, so one clone can appear in several patients. Set cluster_scope = "patient" to search neighbours inside each patient only, which makes clone labels patient-specific. For a single patient the two settings are identical.
  7. Sample integration (conditional). With cluster_scope = "patient", a patient that has more than one sample is harmonised inside that patient only. A batch effect would otherwise split one biological clone into two. This requires the optional harmony package; without it you get a warning and the step is skipped. Global clustering does not integrate.
  8. UMAP. For visualisation only.

4. Reading the QC report 

labels$qc
Column Meaning
n_input Cells before filtering
n_kept Cells that passed
pct_removed Percentage discarded
main_reason Which rule removed the most cells
mito_threshold The mitochondrial cap actually used for this patient
n_clones Clusters found

Plot it to see the fences:

plot_qc_report(
  qc_metrics = labels$qc_metrics,
  kept_cells = labels$cell_labels$cell_id,
  qc_report = labels$qc
)

With many patients, the default pools everyone into three panels (“all metrics”); the per-patient fences are easier to read one metric at a time, which gives one wrapped panel per patient:

plot_qc_report(
  qc_metrics = labels$qc_metrics,
  kept_cells = labels$cell_labels$cell_id,
  qc_report = labels$qc,
  metric = "Detected genes"
)

If a patient loses more than ~50% of its cells, look at the violin plot before trusting the result. The usual causes are a genuinely bad library, or a median that was pulled down by a large low-quality population.

5. From labels to predictions 

prepared <- prepare_data(
  expression_matrix = my_counts,
  clone_labels = labels$cell_labels
)

clone_pred <- predict_drugs(models, prepared$clone_expression_rnorm)
patient_pred <- predict_patients(clone_pred, prepared)

prepared$label_source records where the labels came from ("auto_cluster" in this case), so a result can always be traced back to how its clones were defined.

6. The three ways in

You have Use Labels come from
A raw count matrix preprocess_sc() → prepare_data(clone_labels=) Automatic clustering
A matrix plus clone labels prepare_data(clone_labels=) Your labels
A processed Seurat object prepare_data(data=) Idents() or a metadata column

Nothing is inferred silently: prepare_data() aborts if the assay, the layer, or the patient column cannot be resolved, and lists the available options.

7. What “clone” means here

In the cell-level workflow, clone labels are operationally defined by transcriptomic clustering. Cells are grouped according to transcriptional similarity, and the resulting cluster assignments are used as surrogate clone labels for the downstream model.

With the default global clustering a clone id can occur in several patients: it is a transcriptional state, not a patient-specific subpopulation. Clustering inside each patient (cluster_scope = "patient") gives patient-specific labels instead; the two are identical for a single patient.

These labels do not necessarily represent genetically validated clonal populations, and should not be interpreted as evidence of shared genomic ancestry. CNV or genotype evidence is required to call true clones.

preprocess_sc() marks every cluster with cluster_size_class, which reflects only how many cells it contains:

  • "large": at least min_clone_cells cells (default 10)
  • "small": fewer cells; the cluster is kept, not dropped

The name is deliberately not confidence: a cluster with 50 cells is not more likely to be a real clone than one with 8 cells, it is just larger.

Clusters are never removed automatically:

large_only <- labels$cell_labels[labels$cell_labels$cluster_size_class == "large", ]

8. Reducing non-target cells (optional)

This step is not part of the original PERCEPTION method and is off by default. The original workflow treats every cell you pass in as a candidate clone, so if your matrix is already tumour-cell-only, skip this section.

Tumour tissue contains immune and stromal cells that cluster on their own. Those clusters are not resistance clones, and keeping them dilutes the abundance of real tumour clones. There is a second, less obvious reason: the DepMap models are trained on cancer cell lines, so an immune or fibroblast cluster is out-of-domain input whose predicted viability has no training support. Even so, whether to remove them is a biological decision, not a preprocessing rule – the tumour microenvironment is part of the sample, and in haematological malignancies the “immune” compartment is the tumour.

exclude_markers removes cells that strongly express a programme you want out of the analysis:

labels <- preprocess_sc(
  counts = my_counts,
  patient_labels = cell_to_patient,
  exclude_markers = list(
    immune      = c("PTPRC", "CD3D", "CD3E", "NKG7"),
    myeloid     = c("LYZ", "CD68", "CD14"),
    fibroblast  = c("COL1A1", "DCN", "LUM"),
    endothelial = c("PECAM1", "VWF")
  ),
  exclude_min_expr = 1
)

Each cell is scored by the mean log-normalised expression of every set; if the highest score reaches exclude_min_expr, the cell is removed. The removed cells are returned so the decision stays auditable:

table(labels$excluded_cells$set)

Two warnings about interpretation:

  • This is an exclusion rule, not a tumour-cell classifier. Epithelial markers (EPCAM, KRT8) do not imply malignancy, and some tumours are not epithelial at all.
  • A single marker is weak evidence. Use several genes per set, and inspect the scores in labels$excluded_cells before trusting the filter.

Leaving exclude_markers = NULL (the default) keeps every cell that passed QC.

9. Doublet removal (optional)

Doublets are two cells captured in one droplet. They usually pass QC – a 1:1 doublet has roughly twice the RNA of a singlet but a normal mitochondrial fraction – so the MAD fences cannot see them. A doublet formed from two different clones is especially problematic: it sits between them in the embedding and can become a small cluster read as a distinct resistant clone.

labels <- preprocess_sc(
  counts = my_counts,
  patient_labels = cell_to_patient,
  remove_doublets = TRUE
)
table(labels$doublet_cells$patient)

Detection uses scDblFinder, which is an optional dependency; without it the step warns and is skipped, and the upper gene-count fence still removes most high-complexity doublets. Detection is probabilistic, so the step is off by default. On the 10x PBMC 3k reference it removes ~4-5% of cells, and roughly a quarter of the cells the gene ceiling removes are called doublets.

10. Limitations

  • No ambient RNA correction and no statistical empty-droplet test. Barcodes are separated by the MAD fences plus an absolute gene floor, not by EmptyDrops. On a very dilute library, low-count real cells can therefore be lost together with the empty droplets.
  • No cross-patient integration. Harmony, when used, runs only between samples of the same patient (cluster_scope = "patient"); cells of two different patients are never corrected against each other. Global clustering puts them in one embedding but applies no batch correction.
  • No cell-cycle regression and no cell-type annotation. Clusters are transcriptional groups, not validated clones: CNV or genotype evidence is required before calling clonal ancestry.
  • Doublet removal is optional and probabilistic, and off by default.
